item.title: Voters face uneven AI deepfake protections
item.description:
Data: NCSL; Map: Sara Wise/Axios

Americans across the country could have very different experiences with AI deepfakes leading up to Election Day, thanks to a patchwork of state rules.

Why it matters: AI-generated attack ads and campaign content are rampant leading up to the midterms as candidates across the political spectrum use the technology.

State of play: Twenty-nine states have AI election deepfake laws in effect, while two others — California and Hawaii — have had their laws permanently enjoined, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

  • Minnesota and Texas prohibit political deepfakes for a certain number of days before an election. Maryland's ban is year-round.
  • The other states require disclosures when AI is used in political ads. Some states like Colorado and Utah require more detailed disclosures, such as the deepfake's creator, when it was created and how it was edited.

Friction point: California and Hawaii's AI deepfakes laws were struck down in court on First Amendment grounds.

  • Both states are pressing ahead with alternative approaches that don't specifically regulate election AI deepfakes.
  • California's AI Transparency Act, part of which went into effect on August 3, requires disclosures of AI-generated images and Hawaii last month passed a law prohibiting deepfakes in ads without the subject's consent.

The big picture: At the federal level, lawmakers have yet to establish a baseline standard for election AI deepfakes.

Zoom out: Congress' first AI deepfakes law addressed a different issue.

  • The Take it Down Act, which took effect in May, marked Congress' first attempt at tackling non-consensual intimate imagery — an issue that has collided with election ads targeting women lawmakers.
  • Passing the law was one thing. Implementing it effectively is another, advocates say, citing inconsistent removal processes of posts and predicting litigation will be needed to secure strong enforcement.
  • Lawmakers are also seeking to build on that first step, with House Democrats planning to push legislation next year specifically targeting election deepfakes if they regain power.

The bottom line: Proposals to tackle AI in elections have been floated in Congress for years, but states have moved faster — creating different realities for voters depending on where they live.

item.title: "No escape:" Inside Rubio's Cuba pressure campaign
item.description:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is waging an unprecedented economic war on Cuba — and wants to make sure the island's communist leaders know it's going to get worse.

  • "What we're trying to teach them is, there are no escape valves," Rubio told Axios.

Why it matters: Cuba's economy is in a state of slow-motion collapse because of crushing U.S. sanctions and communist mismanagement of the island, which prides itself as the hemisphere's chief foe of the superpower 90 miles to its north.

  • President Trump hasn't ruled out military action.

Zoom in: Since last year, the Trump administration has taken two dozen separate actions to pressure Cuba. The quantity and extent of the penalties are unique:

  • Sanctioning 40 entities, from foreign companies operating on the island to Cuba's state-run fuel, banking and mining conglomerates.
  • Targeting at least 38 people with economic sanctions, U.S. visa limitations and residency revocations.
  • Pressuring other countries to stop supporting Cuba's doctor-export program, which the State Department calls "human trafficking."
  • Issuing reports attacking Cuba over its human rights record, its failure to fight terrorism and its role in amplifying and assisting anti-capitalist and anti-U.S. political activity.

The big picture: Because of the pressure campaign, Cuba is now a de facto renegade colony of the U.S., upon which it now relies for most of its food, fuel, medicine and currency — all of which are scarce on the island.

  • Cuba's prime minister made a historic announcement Tuesday, saying the government was allowing more private-sector activity than since the Revolution of 1959, the Miami Herald reported.
  • Rubio told Axios that Cuba is playing for time by faking reforms while seeking ways to evade sanctions.
  • "Every time they create a new mechanism in which they try to get out of the noose, we just close it off," Rubio said. "They certainly can't wait us out. Certainly this isn't going to go away for the next 2½ years."

Behind the scenes: Foreign companies are fleeing Cuba amid the threat of sanctions. U.S. companies — especially fuel distributors — are moving in as enterprises such as Cuba's state-run oil company crumble under the pressure. It's creating a nascent capitalist black market.

  • One businessman involved in the fuel trade said some Cuban businesses have even sent human mules to Miami, dripping in heavy gold chains to use as currency because U.S. banking restrictions make financial transactions with Havana impossible.
  • In the first six months of the year, U.S. fuel exports to Cuba jumped to $96 million — more than half of which was in June as the economic forces take their toll, according to the nonprofit U.S.-Cuba Trade and Economic Council.
  • "Trump and Rubio have initiated the most effective sanctions program against a target country than any of their predecessors," said the council's president, John Kavulich. "We've been around since 1994 and never seen anything like this."

Nothing has hurt Cuba as much as Trump's Jan. 3 decision to seize Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro, an island patron like his predecessor, Hugo Chavez, after the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

  • Venezuela supplied Cuba with as much as 100,000 barrels of oil daily. Now, Cuba can barely keep the lights on. It lost a major revenue stream from selling about half of the oil on the global market.
  • "For the first time in Cuba's history, Cuba lacks two things they've always relied on: an outside sponsor and the U.S.'s lack of attention on it as a top priority," Rubio said.
  • "They're not going to get a sponsor in the next 2½ years, so that's the dynamic that's changed," he said. "It's forced them into a very tough spot."

Meanwhile, more lawsuits are being filed after a recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling tied to a law that allows U.S. nationals to sue private companies trafficking in properties seized during the Cuban Revolution.

  • Called the LIBERTAD Act, the law codifies the Cuban embargo, which can be lifted only after Cuba frees political prisoners, guarantees civil rights and has free elections.

Friction point: The U.S embargo against Cuba has long been denounced globally, and accusations of imperialism, particularly from the left, have skyrocketed in the Trump era.

  • Rubio's department essentially framed its critics as useful idiots in its July 20 report, "Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism," which traces the island's espionage and ideological subversion campaigns targeting the U.S.
  • Officials acknowledge the report "lays the groundwork" for more anti-Cuba action. Rubio wouldn't specify what that could be.
  • "If we were to do something with Cuba, you will see the same people who are holding up the pro-Hamas signs and are holding up the 'Release Maduro' signs — they will be out there with the 'Hands Off Cuba' signs," he said.

The other side: Critics say the report fails to catalogue U.S. aggressions against Cuba, exaggerates the island's role as an espionage superpower and wrongly suggests that legitimate complaints about U.S. actions are just Cuban propaganda.

  • "It's a political document. It's not great historical analysis. It's short of a ton of context," said Michael Bustamante, a Cuba historian and University of Miami professor.

The intrigue: Rubio has been in talks to change governance on the island with Raulito Castro, the grandson of ailing Cuban revolutionary Raúl Castro. But it's unclear whether he could lead a transition government or have much staying power.

  • "When Raúl is no longer around, what is his status? Who protects him?" a U.S. official asked.
  • The U.S. is trying to cultivate other Cuban officials and figure out how to create a coalition for reform. But "it's hard to deduce entirely because that system is so paranoid," the official said.
  • Intelligence community officials leaked word Wednesday of a "secret CIA task force" in Cuba, but a senior administration official said there's "nothing new about this beyond letting the regime know we're watching."

What's next: The administration imposed more sanctions Thursday. More are on the way, and Rubio says the administration is in no rush.

  • "One of the things we've lost in American foreign policy and geopolitics is the concept of patience and persistence," he said.
  • "My level of confidence is that when this administration is over, at a minimum, Cuba will be on an irreversible glide path toward a different future."

item.title: Why Max Miller is staying in (for now)
item.description:
Denounced on social media and by fellow Republicans, Ohio Rep. Max Miller is telling allies he's not quitting for a simple reason: It would be tantamount to admitting he beat his ex-wife and their child, which he denies.

Why it matters: The Washington summer scandal is a case study in whether Miller — one of Donald Trump's understudies — can successfully employ the president's playbook of never backing down and never quitting.

  • Trump has publicly expressed sympathy for Miller but privately expressed doubts about his viability.
  • The calls to resign have mounted, especially in the Senate, where Miller's ex-father-in-law, Ohio's Bernie Moreno, serves.

Zoom in: Miller allies say his critics are underestimating his resolve and the intensely personal dynamics of the vicious battle with his ex, Emily Moreno, involving their 2-year-old daughter.

  • "He's really worried about what his daughter is going to think when she gets older," said a congressional colleague.
  • "If he quits, he's basically giving up," the person said. "And if he gives up, it basically means he did it."
  • Also, quitting office or his race would mean surrendering his bully pulpit, which Miller believes he needs to argue his case.

Zoom out: Though some have called for his expulsion from the House, Miller has told his colleagues it would set a terrible precedent because there's no evidence showing he hurt his ex or their child.

  • "Here we are in the middle of a divorce proceeding, and I don't think he's even been charged with anything they're making the accusations of," said an ally, Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tenn.). "We're big on the Constitution, innocent till proven guilty, yet we're guilty until proven innocent, it seems right now with him."
  • House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) called the allegations against Miller "serious" in an interview with Politico on Tuesday but said lawmakers have to allow the Ethics Committee process to play out. "We don't take disciplinary action against members for allegations," Johnson said.
  • Miller has released documents that he says show he was investigated for abuse but that the allegations were unfounded.

Yes, but: There's only so long a candidate can hang on if he's constantly denounced, attacked and looks increasingly un-electable.

  • Republicans privately expect that Miller will drop his reelection bid by the end of this week, according to two sources.

The intrigue: He, his ex and his father-in-law are now embroiled in a dispute over whether the representative held his daughter's blue bunny stuffed animal toy "hostage."

  • Moreno's fellow Republican Ohio senator, Jon Husted, called Thursday for Miller to quit.
  • Another Ohioan, Vice President JD Vance, has an unfriendly relationship with Miller but has pointedly kept quiet.

What's next: According to the Ohio secretary of state office's election calendar, Aug. 10 is the last day that a political party nominating committee can name a replacement for a candidate if he withdraws.

item.title: Inside the GOP's mad dash to recess finish line
item.description:
Senate Republicans are racing toward the August recess with a legislative to-do list worthy of a Joe Rogan podcast: crypto, college sports and hemp.

Why it matters: They likely won't get to all of it, but the White House wants the Senate to get caught trying.

  • First, senators want to get way ahead of any government shutdown fight. Just as important — an NIL rights bill, with ESPN's first College GameDay set for Sept. 5.
  • "I've kind of stacked these things: funding the government, the [Todd] Blanche nomination and the 74 nominations," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said Thursday on Fox News, previewing his agenda.
  • Then come "Russia sanctions, NIL, market structure," he added, rounding out a short list of issues that animate young men, who are the backbone of the MAGA coalition.

What to watch: Thune is still weighing whether and how to force another vote on the SAVE Act or similar election security legislation — even though it's expected to fall well short of the 60 votes needed to advance.

  • "We'll figure out a way to get yet another vote on the Save America Act," Thune told Fox, "but I don't expect the Democrats to change their view."
  • The vote would give Republicans another opportunity to put Democrats on the record opposing a voter ID measure that Thune has called an "80-20 issue."
  • It might also help appease President Trump and his allies in the Senate who are insisting the Senate stay in town until election integrity is addressed.

What we're hearing: If T.S. Eliot covered Congress, he'd decide August is the cruelest month, breeding cloture votes for senators who just want to catch a flight.

  • Some senators remain hopeful for a last-minute deal that would allow Thune to clear the deck and send everyone home Friday.
  • As of Thursday evening, however, the prospect of the Senate working into the weekend remained a real possibility.

The intrigue: One major sticking point is crypto and the CLARITY Act, which would provide the first comprehensive federal regulatory framework for digital assets.

  • Democrats are reluctant to give Republicans an initial procedural vote on the market-structure bill, arguing it could short-circuit bipartisan negotiations and reduce pressure on GOP leaders to come to the table.
  • They are also worried that a failed vote could unlock millions in crypto super PAC money.

Zoom in: Republicans also remain divided over hemp, threatening to complicate passage of the stopgap spending bill.

  • Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) continues to insist on a vote to strip language, inserted at the White House's urging, that would delay implementation of a ban on certain intoxicating hemp products.

item.title: Cyberattacks expose deeper vulnerabilities in U.S. water systems
item.description:
Suspected Iran-linked cyberattacks are exposing long-standing vulnerabilities in fragmented U.S. drinking water systems facing aging infrastructure and intensifying climate threats.

Why it matters: Drinking water systems disruptions can threaten public health and essential services, while many utilities—especially smaller ones—lack the staff and resources to strengthen their defenses..

  • Kevin Morley, federal relations manager for the American Water Works Association (AWWA), tells Axios utilities now have to manage acute cybersecurity threats alongside chronic challenges, including climate change and infrastructure deterioration.

The big picture: There are more than 144,000 public water systems in the U.S., including about 50,000 community water systems that provide drinking water to residents year-round, according to the EPA.

  • That fragmentation across thousands of independently managed utilities makes it harder to modernize infrastructure and maintain consistent cybersecurity standards. It also complicates efforts to prepare for more frequent extreme weather.
  • The biggest challenges aren't unique to the Trump administration, Andrew Whelton, a professor of civil and construction engineering and sustainability engineering at Purdue University, tells Axios.
  • Instead, they reflect infrastructure and funding challenges that have accumulated across successive administrations.
  • Morley says many investment decisions are ultimately made locally because utilities rely heavily on water rates set by municipalities, making politically difficult rate increases a major barrier to replacing aging infrastructure.

Between the lines: Much of America's drinking water infrastructure dates back decades. But Whelton says it's a mistake to think of the sector simply as "old."

  • Many utilities are using replacement projects to redesign systems that can better withstand cyberattacks, wildfires and other disasters.
  • Whelton points to Louisville, Colorado, which redesigned parts of its water system after the 2021 Marshall Fire contaminated the network and caused it to lose pressure.

State of play: Whelton says cybersecurity vulnerabilities have been recognized for decades, but governments have yet to make a sustained effort to strengthen the sector's defenses.

  • Morley says many of today's digital control systems were originally designed for efficiency and reliability — not cybersecurity.
  • The AWWA advocates for the development of nationwide minimum cybersecurity requirements for water utilities, and Morley notes some of the original configurations weren't designed for security.
  • "There's a cultural shift in understanding the reality of the threat and the exposure that's possible," Morley says.
  • AWWA sent a letter to Congress this week urging federal support for utilities as critical infrastructure.

By the numbers: EPA tells Axios it identified vulnerabilities at 277 water systems last year and worked with utilities to address them.

Meanwhile, more frequent extreme weather is forcing utilities to rethink resilience.

  • Whelton says recent wildfires in Washington underscore how utilities that once considered themselves low-risk are now having to prepare for disasters they never expected to face.

Zoom in: Utilities are increasingly balancing investment in cybersecurity with replacing aging pipes, pumps and treatment equipment, even as extreme heat, floods, drought and wildfires place additional stress on water infrastructure.

  • Many community water systems are small operations with only a handful of employees, making it difficult to dedicate staff and funding to cybersecurity.
  • Because most utilities are owned by local governments or special districts, investments in water infrastructure often compete with funding for schools, roads, police and other local priorities.
  • Smaller utilities often depend on state agencies and industry associations for expertise because they lack the staff and resources to tackle cyber threats and climate resilience on their own, Whelton says.

The bottom line: Utilities can no longer afford to think about cyberattacks, climate change and aging infrastructure as separate problems.

  • "Cybersecurity is an acute threat layered on top of chronic challenges," Morley says.

  • The AWWA advocates for the development of nationwide minimum cybersecurity requirements for water utilities, and Morley notes some of the original configurations weren't designed for security.
  • "There's a cultural shift in understanding the reality of the threat and the exposure that's possible," Morley says.
  • AWWA sent a letter to Congress this week urging federal support for utilities as critical infrastructure.

By the numbers: EPA tells Axios it identified vulnerabilities at 277 water systems last year and worked with utilities to address them.

Meanwhile, more frequent extreme weather is forcing utilities to rethink resilience.

  • Whelton says recent wildfires in Washington underscore how utilities that once considered themselves low-risk are now having to prepare for disasters they never expected to face.

Zoom in: Utilities are increasingly balancing investment in cybersecurity with replacing aging pipes, pumps and treatment equipment, even as extreme heat, floods, drought and wildfires place additional stress on water infrastructure.

  • Many community water systems are small operations with only a handful of employees, making it difficult to dedicate staff and funding to cybersecurity.
  • Because most utilities are owned by local governments or special districts, investments in water infrastructure often compete with funding for schools, roads, police and other local priorities.
  • Smaller utilities often depend on state agencies and industry associations for expertise because they lack the staff and resources to tackle cyber threats and climate resilience on their own, Whelton says.

The bottom line: Utilities can no longer afford to think about cyberattacks, climate change and aging infrastructure as separate problems.

  • "Cybersecurity is an acute threat layered on top of chronic challenges," Morley says.

item.title: Author of DNC's 2024 "autopsy" says he concluded Gaza war hurt Harris
item.description:
The author of the Democratic National Committee's 2024 election "autopsy" confirmed an Axios report that he concluded the war in Gaza hurt Kamala Harris politically — and that he'd privately shared that assessment with a pro-Palestinian group.

  • He said he drafted that finding late last year but never submitted it to party leadership.

Why it matters: Democrats have spent months debating whether the Biden administration's support for Israel during its war on Hamas contributed to Harris' defeat.

  • Moderates disputed its electoral significance, while progressives argued that the toll of Israel's war on Gaza civilians drained support from young people, liberals and Arab Americans.

Zoom in: Paul Rivera, who wrote the DNC autopsy, told Axios in an interview that his review of the 2024 election found the war in Gaza cost Harris votes, particularly in Michigan communities with large Arab American populations, such as Dearborn.

  • Rivera, who no longer advises the DNC, this week published his own 564-page report of the 2024 election, which examines the electoral impact of the war in Gaza, among other topics.
  • When the DNC released its autopsy earlier this year, some Democrats criticized it for omitting any discussion of the war in Gaza.
  • In his new document, Rivera concludes that Harris lost tens of thousands of votes in Michigan amid backlash from the Israel-Hamas war, particularly in Dearborn, Dearborn Heights and Hamtramck, where Green Party support surged as activists organized against the Democratic ticket.
  • He contends these losses accounted for a meaningful share of the state's shift toward President Trump, but was only one of several factors behind Harris' defeat in the state.

Rivera wrote that the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the fallout from it in the U.S. is a "complex situation." But, he added, the "political analysis is simple — the electoral results and voting shifts in Michigan and elsewhere demonstrate the impact the crisis had on the Harris campaign."

  • Rivera included in his new report an AP photo of a person holding literature distributed in Michigan in 2024. It read, "Do Not Vote Trump. Do Not Vote Harris. Do Not Vote Genocide."
  • He called it "a warning and a reminder of the stakes for Democrats moving forward."
  • At the same time, he acknowledged that Jewish Americans have faced increasing antisemitism in the U.S. Rivera praised Ken Martin, the DNC's embattled chair, for convening a working group on the Middle East.

The other side: Many moderate Democrats, including those who support Israel, say Gaza's impact on the 2024 election has been overblown.

  • They point to surveys indicating the topic is not among many voters' top concerns.
  • Separate from this issue, Rivera has come under fire from Democrats across the ideological spectrum for what they view more broadly as a botched autopsy.
  • Rivera told the New York Times in a story published this week that he submitted a chapter on other topics that the DNC did not include in its publicly released autopsy. The DNC denied that it was given the chapter.
  • The chapter Rivera claimed he shared with the DNC only briefly mentions the Israel-Palestine conflict, listing it alongside events such as 9/11, the 2008 financial crisis and Hurricane Katrina as occurrences that "have shaped electoral outcomes."

Flashback: Axios reported in February that officials working on the autopsy, which was secret then, had determined that the war in Gaza had eroded support for Harris among some voters — and had told the pro-Palestinian group IMEU Policy Project that in a private meeting.

item.title: Senate panel holds Fauci in contempt over refusal to answer COVID-19 questions
item.description:
A Senate panel voted Thursday to hold Anthony Fauci in contempt for repeatedly declining to answer questions last week from lawmakers investigating the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Why it matters: Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.) has said he will refer the contempt resolution to the Department of Justice for possible prosecution.

  • That could set up a legal clash, since former President Biden preemptively pardoned Fauci before leaving office.

The big picture: The 8-5 vote by the Senate Homeland Security Committee is just one of the ways Republicans are turning up the heat on Fauci.

  • Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) said a subcommittee has obtained the phone Fauci used during the pandemic — providing a potential new flood of revelations after the committee already released his diary.

Driving the news: Paul said Fauci had no reason to invoke his Fifth Amendment right not to answer questions from the Senate committee last week, since Biden had already pardoned him for actions during the time when he led the nation's infectious disease efforts.

  • "Dr. Fauci faced no risk of federal prosecution. All he had to do was tell the truth," Paul said before the vote.
  • Democrats countered that the GOP was trying to put the 85-year-old former top infectious diseases expert in legal jeopardy, by forcing him to make statements that could open new lines of investigation for the committee.
  • Sen. Gary Peters (D-Mich.) said the vote will make it harder to conduct future oversight, because witnesses "will point to this vote as a justification for refusing to appear at all."

Between the lines: The Department of Justice isn't saying whether it will investigate — yet. "The Department seriously reviews all congressional referrals," a DOJ spokesperson said.

At last week's hearing, Fauci said Paul had an "unhinged obsession with me," and was trying to get him to say something that could advance public pledges to put him behind bars.

  • Republicans accused him of trying to evade questions about studies the government funded in China, as well as "gain of function" research they've frequently invoked to support the theory the pandemic originated with a lab leak.

What we're watching: Former Trump advisor Steve Bannon has suggested the Fauci inquiry could resonate politically and help turn out the Republican base, by suggesting government scientists are still captive to pharmaceutical and other special interests.

Go deeper: Fauci woes could deter scientists from public service

Editor's note: This story has been updated to include the DOJ response.

item.title: AI designs new virus not found in nature
item.description:
A Stanford-led research team has used generative AI to design a synthetic virus — the first time artificial intelligence has been harnessed to create a organism that has never been seen in nature.

Why it matters: What could go wrong?

The big picture: It could be the first step toward the nightmare scenario AI experts have already warned about: deadly pathogens that can't be stopped, because they've been created too quickly for our current surveillance systems to stop them.

  • The research could also lead to medical breakthroughs, which is the hope of the research team that conducted the study. "The ability of genome language models to generate entire functional genomes has not been tested," they wrote.

Driving the news: Researchers wrote in Science that they used an AI model to design viruses that can infect and kill the microbe E. coli.

  • While that could go a long way toward controlling deadly bacterial infections, the technology could be harnessed to develop more complex forms of life — and even help design biological weapons.

The intrigue: The news also throws a new twist into government efforts to regulate high-risk research.

  • The Trump administration has been focused on "gain of function" research on natural pathogens — as has Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), whose committee held Anthony Fauci in contempt Thursday for refusing to answer questions from lawmakers investigating the origins of the COVID-19 pandemic.
  • But the AI work created something entirely new. It goes way beyond just studying how to manipulate natural viruses.

Between the lines: Biotechnology is regulated through a patchwork of laws and agencies, with breakthroughs frequently outpacing regulators.

  • The Trump administration last month issued a policy for stopping high-risk research in the life sciences that prohibits federally funded "gain of function" research and calls for enhanced oversight of projects involving harmful biological agents.
  • But that didn't specifically address AI-driven research, which is evolving at breakneck speeds.

What they're saying: Johns Hopkins health security experts Thomas Inglesby and Moritz Hanke, writing in the same issue of Science, praised the Stanford team for taking precautions, but said there aren't enough existing guardrails to oversee generative genomics.

  • "The ability to compose viral genomes using generative AI now exists; the governance to safely steer it does not," they wrote.

item.title: FCC votes to lift broadcast ownership cap
item.description:
The FCC on Thursday voted 2-1 to eliminate the national TV ownership cap rule that bars a single broadcaster from owning stations that reach more than 39% of U.S. TV households.

Why it matters: The party-line vote clears the way for local broadcasters to merge, giving single broadcast ownership groups far more reach than they previously could have.

  • FCC chairman Brendan Carr has long argued that the cap was outdated and limits the ability of broadcasters to consolidate to compete with tech firms and streamers.

Zoom in: The FCC said in a statement that deals would be evaluated on a case-by-case basis that authorizes deals that satisfy the agency's public review standard.

  • "This will empower the FCC to approve deals that promote the public interest while allowing the agency to reject any deals that do not meet that standard," it said.

What they're saying: In a statement, a Nexstar spokesperson said "For too long, local broadcasters were handcuffed from reaching the scale they needed to compete on a more level playing field."

  • "Modernizing these rules will help ensure broadcasters can continue investing in local journalism and providing the free, trusted news and information that communities across America rely on every day."

Between the lines: Nexstar is the clearest example of a beneficiary of the raised cap.

  • Its $6.2 billion takeover of rival Tegna is currently on pause as a federal judge considers an antitrust lawsuit filed by DirecTV and several state attorneys general.
  • The FCC's Media Bureau approved Nexstar's application to transfer Tegna's broadcast licenses without a full, public commission vote in March.

Reality check: Thursday's vote to lift the cap doesn't resolve the antitrust lawsuit that put the deal on pause.

  • That suit addresses issues outside of the FCC's cap vote.
  • DirecTV says the deal would allow Nexstar to have pricing leverage over pay-TV distributors and those costs would be passed on to consumers.
  • There's an ongoing debate over whether the FCC has the authority to lift the cap.

Context: FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez — the lone Democrat — voted in dissent, arguing Congress removed the FCC's authority to adjust the ownership cap after approving the current limit in 2004.

  • The Biden-era FCC opposed lifting the cap, and the FCC killed Tegna's $5.4 billion attempt to combine with Standard General in 2023.

What's next: The vote will likely be met with legal resistance by consumer advocacy groups.

  • Already, Free Press, a media advocacy non-profit, said it plans to appeal the vote.

item.title: Trump targets birth tourism and citizenship in new executive orders
item.description:
President Trump plans to sign two executive orders Thursday seeking to narrow birthright citizenship in several circumstances and intensify the federal crackdown on commercial "birth tourism," Axios has learned.

  • Trump also is seeking to deny birthright citizenship for children born of some foreign diplomatic staff in the U.S. and, potentially, U.S. territories in the future.

Why it matters: It's Trump's second attempt to curb birthright citizenship in the U.S. and is sure to be challenged in court as a violation of the 14th Amendment, which guarantees citizenship to nearly everyone born in America.

  • The U.S. Supreme Court on June 30 shot down a broader executive order Trump signed on Inauguration Day to deny automatic citizenship to those born of noncitizens in the U.S.

Zoom in: Trump's administration argues that the ruling still grants him the authority to limit birthright citizenship under long-standing exceptions recognized by the court. The executive orders apply only to future births tied to four categories:

  1. Children born of foreign diplomatic staff working on behalf of another government while in the U.S. The 14th Amendment doesn't confer automatic citizenship to ambassadors' families, and this order would expand that category to other noncitizen employees.
  2. Children of people who are classified as alien enemies, including those who belong to federally declared terrorist groups. The 14th Amendment doesn't apply to invading armies, and this designation would expand that category.
  3. Those born in U.S. territories — but only if Congress changes the law to end automatic citizenship there. A bill seeking to do that was introduced last month but isn't expected to pass. This would apply most notably to those in Puerto Rico.
  4. Children born of mothers who expressly and deceptively enter the U.S. for the sole purpose of having a child here, namely at a birth-tourism center. The order seeks to limit the use of surrogate mothers for this purpose as well.

Between the lines: The administration argues that creating this birth-tourism exception is permitted because of parents' fraudulent misrepresentation in gaining access to the U.S., typically as tourists or workers.

  • The government can revoke the citizenship of those naturalized by fraud. The new order says this exception now applies to a mother if she deceptively engages in the commercial practice of birth tourism, officials say.

A second executive order directs the secretary of state and the Department of Homeland Security secretary to issue rules and guidance to stop birth tourism and target the industry at home and abroad.

  • U.S. law already bans getting a tourist visa "for the primary purpose of obtaining U.S. citizenship for a child by giving birth in the United States."
  • Immigration officials also can deny a pregnant foreign national from entering the U.S. if they determine she's entering the country for the purpose of giving birth.

The intrigue: The House Oversight Committee is investigating birth tourism centers and in May requested a host of documents from a company called "Have My Baby in Miami."

  • "The benefits of U.S. citizenship are a unique privilege," the committee wrote.
  • "However, as foreign expectant mothers traveling for this purpose come predominantly from China and Russia, there are concerns that the birth tourism industry is giving rise to potential national security and election integrity threats posed by adversarial nations that challenge U.S. interests."
  • The Senate Homeland Security Committee also released a 2022 report on birth tourism.

By the numbers: Estimates about the number of children who've been the result of birth tourism range from the low thousands to the tens of thousands.

What they're saying: Trump has focused heavily on birth tourism as part of his so-far unsuccessful push to limit birthright citizenship more broadly.

  • "Birthright citizenship is not about rich people from China, and the rest of the World, who want their children, and hundreds of thousands more, FOR PAY, to ridiculously become citizens of the United States of America," he wrote March 30 on Truth Social.
  • His critics said then that he should focus on just that.
  • "If birth tourism is a problem, the answer is to enforce that regulation," Amanda Frost, a University of Virginia immigration law professor, told PolitiFact in an analysis.

item.title: McConnell discharged from rehab center, Senate return still unclear
item.description:
Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) was discharged from a rehab facility and has returned home amid his lengthy absence from Congress, he said in a statement released Thursday by his office.

The big picture: The 84-year-old lawmaker was hospitalized in June and has not been seen in public since, outside of images released by his office.

  • The mystery of McConnell's continued absence has fueled questions about his capacity to serve the remainder of his term, which ends in January 2027.

Driving the news: "On the advice of my doctors, I'll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period, and I'll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business," McConnell said in his statement.

  • The GOP stalwart, who is currently serving his seventh term, confirmed last month that he was hospitalized following a fall and was "briefly unconscious."
  • Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat, has demanded McConnell demonstrate his fitness to carry out his term or resign.

The bottom line: McConnell did not provide any indication of when he would be returning to the Hill — where his absence has complicated Republicans' political math.

Go deeper: Scoop: Democrat wants reckoning over McConnell, Kean absences

item.title: Jan. 6 prosecutions are over, but the fight lingers
item.description:
The years-long saga of prosecuting the Jan. 6 attack effectively came to an end this week, when a judge dismissed a remaining indictment against Oath Keepers members already freed by President Trump.

The big picture: Not only has Trump erased the legal consequences for many Jan. 6 defendants, but his administration has moved to rewrite the history of a deadly day — and oust federal employees who worked on related cases.

Driving the news: Judges in recent weeks disposed of the final two cases accusing leaders of the Proud Boys and Oath Keepers of orchestrating a plot to undermine the transfer of power. But the jurists were candid in saying that didn't mean they agreed with the administration.

  • Judge Amit Mehta acknowledged the gravity of his Tuesday order granting the DOJ's request to toss the Oath Keepers' indictment. "This is the last of the prosecutions seeking to hold accountable those responsible for the events of January 6," he wrote. "That book is now closed."
  • He wrote of an epilogue that diminished what happened that day and denigrated the work of prosecutors and law enforcement. But he concluded, "The court cannot write a different ending."
  • A DOJ spokesperson told Axios in a statement that they "respect" Mehta's decision but "disagree with the characterization of our reasoning."

Zoom out: U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee, similarly dismissed the remaining Proud Boys' case but recognized Jan. 6 "was an attack on the Constitution's mechanism to facilitate the peaceful transfer of power from one president to the next."

What they're saying: But even if the prosecutions have ended, they've created an in-depth chronicle of that day and what led to it, says Brendan Ballou, founder of the Public Integrity Project and a former federal prosecutor who resigned from the DOJ following the Jan. 6 pardons.

  • "This was this was always a risk, and why I think the prosecutions were so important," Ballou tells Axios. "Because it's a historical record that, try as he might, Donald Trump is not successfully erasing."

Catch up quick: In those high-profile cases, members of both groups were found guilty of seditious conspiracy.

  • Henry "Enrique" Tarrio, who led the Proud Boys, was sentenced to 22 years in prison, the longest sentence handed down in the Jan. 6 cases. Stewart Rhodes, of Oath Keepers infamy, was sentenced to 18 years.
  • But Tarrio was pardoned in Trump's day-one clemency sweep, while other members of the far-right groups had their sentences cut short with commutations. Earlier this year, the DOJ asked an appeals court to vacate the remaining convictions.

Between the lines: The end of the cases comes as no great surprise under an administration that's taken a radically different approach to Jan. 6 than its predecessors.

  • Even with his $1.776 billion "anti-weaponization" fund defunct, the president has continued to suggest those involved in the riot deserve payouts.
  • The controversy has also spilled out into the way Trump's judicial nominees have talked about the riot after years of prosecutions and Capitol Hill probes, sparking Democratic ire and warnings from former DOJ attorneys who prosecuted Jan. 6 cases.
  • "Anybody that has interacted with the reality of January six knows that it was an attack on democracy," Ballou says.

Go deeper: Jan. 6 officers sue over Trump's $1.8B fund they call a "corrupt sham"

item.title: Trump backs Hegseth, calls reports to the contrary "treasonous"
item.description:
President Trump on Thursday publicly defended Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and said reporting suggesting any friction between the two was "treasonous."

Why it matters: The Washington Post and others reported this week that Trump had reached his limits with Hegseth over the state of the country's weapons stockpile and the impact on the war with Iran.

What they're saying: "The Fake News, as usual, is spreading false and completely unfounded rumors. I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing," Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday.

  • "Pete is highly respected within the Military, and has made tremendous improvements, including getting rid of DEI, and increasing recruitment to historic levels," the post read.
  • "This rumor was started by The Washington ComPost, one of the worst Media Outlets in the business, despite our telling them their story is completely FALSE. In actuality, I really believe their fake "reporting" is treasonous!"
  • A representative for The Washington Post did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Catch up quick: The Post, citing sources familiar, reported that Trump vented at Hegseth over the country's dwindling munitions stockpile that could hamstring military operations against Iran.

  • Over the weekend, the president announced that he called off a potential attack on Iran — later saying he canceled what would've been "the biggest attack since World War II" — due to progress in negotiations.
  • But reporting from The Post suggested weaponry shortages were part of the reason Washington had refrained from launching new attacks.
  • Trump argued after midnight Thursday — following other reports that the U.S. was low on certain precision missiles — that the military has "massive amounts" of munitions and said "large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information throughout.

item.title: Trump may get a big, new tariff authority
item.description:
A legal cat-and-mouse game has played out over whether the president can use various obscure, untested provisions to impose tariffs. Now, Congress appears on track to give him a big, new — and explicit — tariff authority.

Why it matters: A bill on Russia sanctions, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, has received overwhelming bipartisan support in the Senate and would allow President Trump and future presidents to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major importers of Russian energy.

  • If enacted in its current form, it would give the president greater flexibility to raise import taxes on major economies including India, China and the European Union, without the legal limits and ambiguity of the tools he has used thus far.

Catch up quick: The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 passed a key procedural hurdle in the Senate last week by an 86-12 vote.

  • It strengthens sanctions on Russia and Iran and targets Russia's "shadow fleet" of oil tankers used to avoid Russian sanctions, and imposes a 500% tariff on U.S. imports from Russia.
  • The bill states that the U.S. trade representative can adjust tariff rates to anywhere between 0% and 100% on the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas by volume.
  • The trade representative must merely notify Congress about its actions; there are no further constraints or requirements needed for the administration to justify whatever tariff rate it chooses.

State of play: It comes as Trump's broader tariff agenda has faced challenges and setbacks in the courts.

  • The Supreme Court ruled against Trump's use of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act to impose sweeping tariffs, and the Treasury has refunded $100 billion to importers who paid them.
  • The administration then turned to Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, allowing temporary tariffs to address balance-of-payments deficits. That provision limits the scale and duration of tariffs, and a lower court struck down its use anyway.

The intrigue: The administration most recently turned to Section 301 of the Trade Act, allowing tariffs as retaliation for unfair practices by trading partners.

  • That is a tried-and-true provision that has been used across many presidential administrations, but the specific grounds for its invocation in this case is more dubious, asserting that retaliation is needed for forced labor practices in some of the wealthiest countries on earth.
  • Businesses that face the import taxes are challenging those in court, as well.

Between the lines: If enacted in its current form, the Russia sanctions legislation would grant the president a more legally bulletproof tool to impose much higher tariffs, at least on a handful of major economies.

  • There's nothing in the bill's text that compels Trump or future presidents to tie the use of the tariffs to some specific geostrategic goal involving Russia's war with Ukraine.

What they're saying: "The sentiment is obviously right," Jonathan Finer, former principal deputy national security adviser, tells Axios. "The war won't end until [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is pressured enough to stop. But the details matter."

  • "The bill includes no sanctions authorities the president doesn't already have, lets him off the hook with a waiver to avoid using them, and gives him enormous authorities to tariff U.S. partners and allies up to 100%, largely at his discretion," Finer said.

item.title: More Americans say extreme heat is affecting their lives
item.description:
Reproduced from AP; Chart: Axios Visuals

Greater shares of Americans now say that extreme heat has affected various parts of day-to-day life compared to just two years ago.

Why it matters: The findings, from the AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, suggest that people are increasingly aware of extreme heat's impact on their health, budgets, travel plans and more.

By the numbers: 90% of Americans now say that extreme heat has had at least a minor impact on their lives broadly, up from 83% two years ago.

  • 80% now say that extreme heat has had at least a minor impact on their power bills, up from 69% in 2024.
  • 68% say it's affecting their outdoor activities, up from 57%.
  • 42% say it's affecting their travel or vacation plans, up from 26%.
A youth football coach sweats amid a July 2026 heat wave in Chicago. Photo: Octavio Jones/AFP via Getty Images

Zoom in: The shifts were driven in part by people living in the West and Midwest, both of which have recently been hit by dangerous and deadly extreme heat events.

  • There's also a partisan divide, with Democrats more likely than Republicans to say that heat has had a major impact on the parts of life included in the survey.

Between the lines: Researchers have found that climate change is making extreme heat events more frequent and more intense.

  • Yet the share of Americans who say that climate change is happening is dropping: 66% said so in this latest survey, down from 73% last year.

How it works: The poll of 1,165 adults was conducted July 23-27, 2026, with a margin of error of +-3.7 percentage points.

item.title: Welcome to the singularity: AI's architects say the next era of human history is here
item.description:
Top AI architects say their technology has arrived at a threshold once confined to science fiction: the singularity, or the moment machines begin accelerating their own evolution.

Why it matters: If these moguls are right, we may be entering the most consequential technological transition in human history — the opening stages of an "intelligence explosion" that transforms civilization faster than humanity can understand or control.

Driving the news: Google jolted the tech world Wednesday by announcing a sweeping rupture in the brain trust that built its modern AI empire, as its leaders signaled that artificial general intelligence (AGI) is within reach.

  • DeepMind founder and CEO Demis Hassabis, who has declared we're "standing in the foothills of the singularity," is handing over day-to-day control of the lab to become Alphabet's chief scientist and chair of Google DeepMind, focusing on the future of AGI.
  • Google chief scientist Jeff Dean and several top researchers are leaving to launch Discovery Loop, a startup aimed at accelerating — and eventually automating — machine-learning research and scientific discovery.

Zoom out: The upheaval offers the clearest institutional evidence yet that AI's architects see something extraordinary approaching.

  • "We are now, like, in the singularity," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on the "Relentless" podcast last month. "I've been waiting for this my whole life."
  • Elon Musk, Altman's fiercest rival, has been making the same argument since January. Last week, he doubled down: "AI is already superhuman at many things. We are in the singularity."
  • Anthropic, whose CEO Dario Amodei prefers the term "the AI exponential," says Claude is already helping build more powerful AI and could soon automate nearly all AI research and engineering.

The big picture: The industry has yet to achieve full "recursive self-improvement" (RSI), the point at which AI can repeatedly help build increasingly powerful successors with minimal human guidance.

  • Humans still select research goals, validate results and oversee the enormous computing infrastructure required to train frontier models.
  • Yet pieces of the loop are beginning to fall into place.

What's changed: Frontier models are beginning to automate research, produce original discoveries and display forms of autonomy associated with the early stages of an intelligence explosion.

  • OpenAI, which released GPT-5.6 in July, spent last week briefing officials in Washington on Astra, an even more powerful model that the company says has solved or substantially advanced 10 long-standing problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science.

The intrigue: The breakthroughs have come with unsettling signs of autonomous behavior.

  • During an unusually permissive cyber evaluation, an Anthropic agent created fake identities and tried to manipulate a real developer into approving malicious code, the U.K.'s AI Security Institute revealed Tuesday.
  • No known harm resulted. But the episode followed several cases in which OpenAI and Anthropic models reached real systems during testing — including a breach Altman said he "felt very viscerally."

Follow the money: Labs and investors are increasingly organizing around the possibility that AI's self-improvement loop is beginning to close.

  • Lilian Weng recently left her role as a co-founder of Thinking Machines Lab to lead work on recursive self-improvement at OpenAI.
  • Richard Socher's Recursive Superintelligence has raised hundreds of millions of dollars to pursue self-improving AI.
  • Discovery Loop plans to use its automated research system first to improve its own AI architectures — with backing and computing power from Google and funding led by Khosla Ventures and Radical Ventures.

Reality check: Even a rapid intelligence explosion inside the labs could take far longer to transform daily life.

  • Companies must redesign workflows, governments must develop expertise, and workers must decide when to trust systems whose capabilities are changing faster than institutions can evaluate them.
  • "Our democracies, economies, and legal systems weren't built to absorb AI at the rate it's advancing," Blaise Agüera y Arcas, Google CTO of technology and society, said in a post Monday.

The bottom line: Futurists have predicted the singularity for decades. Today, the architects of frontier AI increasingly believe its event horizon is already behind us.

item.title: Schumer's path to the majority runs through his Democratic critics
item.description:
On a good day, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer can see a Democratic majority in 2027.

Why it matters: On a bad one, he can see the caucus that comes with it.

  • Abdul El-Sayed's 48.5% to 47.5% victory over Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) exposed an uncomfortable reality for Schumer: Some of the Democrats most likely to deliver him a majority may also be the hardest to lead.
  • "If you're Chuck Schumer, I'm dangerous," El-Sayed said during the campaign. "If you're AIPAC, I'm dangerous. If you're a corporate PAC, I'm dangerous."

Driving the news: Schumer was quick to endorse El-Sayed Wednesday, like he did after Graham Platner clobbered his preferred candidate in Maine.

  • "We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November," Schumer and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, chair of the Democratic Senate campaign arm, said in a joint statement.
  • El-Sayed didn't directly comment on the endorsement Wednesday. "There's a lot of healing to do after a hard-fought primary like this," he said. "Always magnanimity in victory."

What we're watching: The next test for Schumer comes Aug. 11 in Minnesota, where voters will choose between progressive favorite Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and Rep. Angie Craig (D-Minn.), the preferred choice of the Democratic establishment.

  • It's the Minnesota Nice version of the ugly proxy war between the party's two wings — with a twist. Unlike in Michigan or Maine, the Democratic nominee is all but certain to win in November.
  • Flanagan, who leads in the polls, has declined to say whether she'd support Schumer for Democratic leader.
  • Ditto Democrats' Texas nominee, state Rep. James Talarico, who has called for "new blood" in Washington.
  • El-Sayed backs progressive Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) who "has shown what effective leadership in the Senate looks like."

Zoom out: Schumer's problem is one most minority leaders would envy: He has several paths to the majority, even if he ends up with a few more detractors.

  • And he isn't overly concerned with candidates declining to pledge support for him before Election Day. His mantra: Just win.
  • Two of the Democrats' best pick-up opportunities are Ohio and Alaska, where Schumer personally recruited former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) to run.
  • And neither Rep. Chris Pappas in New Hampshire nor former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina — who are both leading in polls — are anti-leadership firebrands.

The bottom line: Schumer finds himself in the same boat as the man he wants to dethrone: Majority Leader John Thune.

  • Both will have freshman senators who owe their victories—and perhaps their loyalties—to political movements and constituencies beyond their orbit.
  • But Schumer may have the better insurance policy. No one has expressed any public interest in the job.

  • Two of the Democrats' best pick-up opportunities are Ohio and Alaska, where Schumer personally recruited former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) to run.
  • And neither Rep. Chris Pappas in New Hampshire nor former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina — who are both leading in polls — are anti-leadership firebrands.

The bottom line: Schumer finds himself in the same boat as the man he wants to dethrone: Majority Leader John Thune.

  • Both will have freshman senators who owe their victories—and perhaps their loyalties—to political movements and constituencies beyond their orbit.
  • But Schumer may have the better insurance policy. No one has expressed any public interest in the job.

item.title: "Entrapment": Trump's immigration delays fuel jump in ICE arrest targets
item.description:
A work slowdown by the Trump administration's immigration offices has exploded the backlog of applications for citizenship, green cards and work permits to an unprecedented 7.5 million people, according to the latest agency data.

  • Add the millions of immigrants waiting on decisions for asylum, work visas and permission to stay in the U.S. for humanitarian reasons, and the total backlog soars to more than 12.1 million.

Why it matters: The delays have put potentially millions of people in legal immigration limbo — vulnerable to being arrested by ICE agents and deported, even if they've followed the rules to try to stay in the U.S.

  • Officials say the delays are being driven by the administration's new focus on stricter vetting. A wave of DOGE-induced retirements also reduced the workforce at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS).
  • Critics, however, see a calculated plan to boost arrests and deportations by slowing approvals to put more immigrants in legal jeopardy.

It's "like a form of entrapment," said Sarah Pierce, a former policy analyst at USCIS and now director of social policy at Third Way.

  • "This administration is using all of the tools at their disposal to make more individuals vulnerable to deportation."

Zoom in: People with pending applications — including those who entered the U.S. legally — are being arrested while traveling domestically through airports such as those in Philadelphia and Denver.

  • Unauthorized immigrants who've married U.S. citizens and apply to adjust their immigration status are being arrested at their application interviews.
  • Even refugees, who are eligible to apply for permanent residency after one year of living in the U.S., are being targeted for ICE detention while their cases are processed — a reversal from previous practice.

What they're saying: The delays ensure that "these individuals are vulnerable to detention and deportation for longer, giving [ICE] a larger pool of individuals to pull from to increase this administration's deportation numbers," Pierce said.

  • USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said in a statement that the agency "remains committed to reducing case backlogs through a deliberate, data-driven, and risk-informed approach that strengthens both efficiency and the integrity of the nation's legal immigration system." 
  • "By using new technology and smarter processes, we can focus on stopping criminals, fraud and abuse, and make sure we apply the law as Congress intended," he added.

The big picture: The administration has consistently said it planned to increase vetting and scrutiny on all types of applications at USCIS.

  • But the consequence of such a large backlog and pauses on some cases — a practice that's being challenged in court — has put millions of immigrants who normally wouldn't be priorities onto ICE's radar.
  • "I think they've kind of ran out of easy (deportation) targets, and so that's why cases are piling up," said Mike Watkins, a former USCIS supervisor who left the agency last year.

Zoom out: There were about 2 million more people waiting on case decisions this June compared to June 2024, according to the agency's monthly data report on six application types, including citizenship, permanent residency and work authorization.

  • More than 5.6 million people have been waiting for more than six months for a decision in those categories.
  • There's also a "frontlog" of 38,500 unopened immigration applications of all types, as of March 31. And there's about 7 million active cases that have been designated as taking longer than USCIS's standard to resolve.

By the numbers: Processing times for citizenship applications (called naturalization) doubled from five months to about 10 months between June 2024 and June 2026.

  • Cubans seeking permanent residency are having to wait more than 21 months for a decision, up from about six months two years ago.
  • USCIS stopped sharing wait times for DACA work authorization applications last year.
  • But "Dreamers" — who were brought to the U.S. as unauthorized children and now are trying to renew their work authorization — are in an immigration category in which 1.3 million people have been waiting more than six months for a decision on whether they can stay.
  • Two years ago, the number was 556,000.

"People that have done nothing wrong — they followed the rules, they've done everything that's asked of them — (but) because of processing delays, they're being made to suffer," said Watkins, who now runs his own immigration law practice.

item.title: Climate change is fueling wildfire risk — and anxiety
item.description:
SEATTLE — Wildfire smoke blanketing this coastal city and much of the West is bringing an ominous reminder that the reach of destructive fires is growing.

Why it matters: Climate scientists study how global warming increases the odds of wildfire. People living through it are confronting a more immediate question: where is truly safe anymore?

The big picture: Wildfires intensified by climate change are like an unforgiving spotlight sweeping across the world. No one really knows where it will stop next.

Driving the news: Right now, that spotlight is on Spokane, Washington, where a historic wildfire has destroyed neighborhoods and remains uncontrolled. Fires are also burning in the Bordeaux region in France, outside Madrid and in British Columbia.

  • "I don't think we've had one single year in the past decade where there hasn't been at least one catastrophic fire event of some magnitude that looks just like this," said climate scientist Daniel Swain, in a virtual presentation Monday showing Spokane neighborhoods burned to the ground.

Catch up quick: Catastrophic fires have repeatedly destroyed populated communities:

  • Fort McMurray, Alberta (2016); Santa Rosa, California (2017); Paradise, California (2018); Australia's "Black Summer" (2019-20); Oregon Labor Day fires that reached the edge of Portland (2020); Denver suburbs of Louisville and Superior, Colorado (2021); Lahaina, Hawaii (2023); Pacific Palisades, California (2025).

My thought bubble: Tragically, we must add Spokane to that list. The fires were a wake-up call for my parents, who live in another part of the city near forested land.

  • We didn't talk about climate change. We talked about evacuation plans and how quickly they could get their cats into carriers.

Reality check: Climate change doesn't cause wildfires, which have always been part of nature. Spokane itself suffered a devastating wildfire in 1991.

  • But climate change is creating hotter weather and drier vegetation that make wildfires larger and more intense.
  • Meanwhile, population growth into fire-prone landscapes is also increasing exposure.

Threat level: When those latent trends intersect with highly variable factors — high winds, lightning or even a suspected arsonist, such as in Spokane — devastating fires are ignited.

What they're saying: "Wildfires may look random on a map, but they're rarely random from a risk perspective," said Firas Saleh, who directs wildfire models at Moody's.

  • Places as varied as Spokane, France and Hawaii share hotter temperatures, longer fire seasons, more burnable vegetation and growing development in fire-prone landscapes, Saleh said.

Between the lines: Climate change is only one factor behind destructive fires, making direct attribution difficult — and often beside the point for people living through them.

  • Susan Prichard, a forest ecologist at the University of Washington, said she wonders if the scientific community made a mistake assuming people would become more concerned about climate change as extreme weather — made worse due to climate change — becomes more common.

"I'm not a social scientist, but I do know through lived experience that saying 'it's getting so bad, are you now going to be part of the solution?' doesn't seem to work," said Prichard, who has evacuated from the small town where she lives in the Cascade foothills in Washington, five times in the last 20 years due to wildfires.

Zoom in: A few days after Saturday's onslaught of fires, I asked my parents if they had thought about climate change. Not really, they said, as they were still focused on the crisis at hand, though they added they also see the climate connection. "I just want summer to be over," my mother said.

  • That is an increasingly common refrain in these parts, unfortunately.

"That's a form of coping: How do we manage the terror and dread of it all?" said Claire Rapp, a Colorado State University scientist specializing in behavior science and wildfires.

  • Once the immediate crisis passes, Rapp recommends developing an evacuation plan and improving household preparedness while recognizing that climate change is increasing overall wildfire risk.

Zoom out: More Americans say they've personally experienced climate change as heat, wildfire smoke and floods become more common, according to Yale University research.

  • But recognizing climate change and thinking about it in the middle of a disaster are two very different things.

What we're watching: That disconnect helps explain why two conversations increasingly happen in parallel: One about near-term adaptation and another about long-term climate mitigation.

  • Cutting greenhouse gas emissions matters over decades, but it doesn't help someone deciding whether to evacuate tonight.

What's next: More wildfires, I'm afraid.

The bottom line: "It's just early August," said Prichard. "Some fires that are burning will not be put out until rain and snow hits them, and it's just a long way to go until then."

item.title: House GOP scandals expand Democrats' 2026 map
item.description:
Four scandal-plagued House Republicans whose seats should be gimmes for the GOP have instead turned their races into unexpected battlegrounds. Why it matters: These aren't districts you'd expect to be in play — Donald Trump carried all four comfortably in 2024. But the incumbents' ethical troubles are making Republicans spend time and money defending the seats — in a cycle where neither party has any room for error.

Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) dropped his reelection bid after the Ethics Committee found he violated House rules by sexually harassing female aides and creating a hostile work environment. That's set off a scramble to find a replacement just three months before the election.

  • The race was shifted to "toss-up" last week by Sabato's Crystal Ball, even before the ethics report was released. Trump won Edwards' district by 9.5 points last cycle.
  • Whoever North Carolina Republicans choose on Monday night to replace Edwards will have a short runway to fundraise and introduce themselves to the district.

Max Miller (R-Ohio) is accused of assaulting his ex-wife and their child, allegations he denies.

  • Even Trump expressed doubts to Miller that he can win, Axios reported this week. But he's been defiant amid calls for him to drop out.
  • Democrats are pinning their hopes on ironworker Brian Poindexter, a progressive populist backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).
  • Trump carried the district by 11 points two years ago.

Cory Mills (R-Fla.) remains under an active Ethics Committee investigation over allegations that center on domestic abuse, stolen valor and financial misconduct, all of which he denies.

  • Trump won Mills' district by 13 points in 2024, but Mills is facing a tough primary fight.
  • Reps. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) and Mike Haridopolos (R-Fla.) officially backed Mills' primary challenger, Ryan Elijah. Haridopolos told Axios Wednesday that Elijah is a "true family man who can win in November in this safe Republican seat."
  • Multiple Democrats are vying to challenge Mills, but party leadership has lined up behind former NASA Chief of Staff Bale Dalton.

Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.) had his phone seized by the FBI in 2024 as part of an investigation into his campaign finances.

  • The Justice Department dropped the case after Trump returned to office last year, but the probe has left Ogles politically vulnerable.
  • Democratic leadership's top-flight recruit in the district, Columbia Mayor Chaz Molder, has a 3-to-1 fundraising advantage over Ogles.

What they're saying: Viet Shelton, a spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC), projected confidence that all four of these districts are very much in play.

  • "Vulnerable House Republicans mistakenly think that no matter how awful their behavior is, they are untouchable," he said in a statement.
  • "Voters in these districts are pissed over higher costs, Republicans' broken promises, and are ready to reject these scandal-plagued members, who've made voters' lives worse."

Between the lines: There's a chance Ogles, Mills and Miller don't make it to the general election.

  • Ogles and Mills are both facing primary challenges from GOP rivals who have out-raised them.
  • Miller has until next week to withdraw from the ballot and Republicans are eyeing contingency plans in case he bows to growing pressure.

The bottom line: "If all four of them are on the ballot, it's a lot more of a pain in the ass," one GOP operative told Axios shortly before Edwards dropped his bid.

item.title: How OpenAI's agents broke out of testing to hack Hugging Face
item.description:
Weeks before OpenAI's agents hacked Hugging Face, the agents worked together to find and exploit a vulnerability in the infrastructure supporting the company's cybersecurity testing, OpenAI researchers said Wednesday.

Why it matters: The new findings raise questions about how frontier AI labs are monitoring their testing environments — and the challenges safety testers are finding as they try to rein in increasingly powerful AI.

Driving the news: OpenAI's internal research model, one of the models involved in the Hugging Face breach, first discovered and exploited a vulnerability in Artifactory, a third-party file repository connected to the company's testing sandbox, on May 26, two researchers said at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference on Wednesday.

  • The genius-level actions observed in testing showed exactly what could happen if these models make it to the hands of hackers.
  • "We believe this is a watershed moment for computer security as an industry, as well as for OpenAI as a whole," Michael Dalton, a member of OpenAI's technical staff, said during the presentation.

What happened: OpenAI started testing its internal research model, which is not intended for public release, on May 7.

  • Within a day, after getting stuck while trying to complete a cybersecurity evaluation, the model reasoned that it could reach the internet indirectly. The model then discovered it could write its own files in Artifactory's shared package repository.
  • It then left a note to other agents about its discovery.
  • Soon, more agents started leaving notes for each other in the repository, creating a de facto message board where the agents collaborated and traded information about their findings, including new vulnerabilities they found.

Zoom in: The agents uncovered a variety of vulnerabilities in Artifactory, including a remote code execution flaw and another that gave them administrator privileges.

  • When the agent found the privileges flaw, it thought, "Holy shit reader is ADMIN? We can read config/users! Earlier assumed not due to [user experience]," according to a slide in the presentation detailing the agent's thought process while completing its test.

The intrigue: In early July, a few days before the Hugging Face incident, the agents overloaded the Artifactory service and caused an outage. The outage prompted an internal OpenAI investigation showing that the agents' compromised the repository.

  • OpenAI then cleared the message board and patched the zero-day in Artifactory that the agents were exploiting by July 6.
  • OpenAI believed it had fixed the problem after the July 4 incident and resumed training.

Two days later, the agents recreated the message board through a completely different mechanism.

  • The agents then began coordinating more aggressively, using Artifactory's internet access to pursue external infrastructure they believed might contain answers to their evaluation tasks.
  • That collaboration ultimately culminated in the compromise of Hugging Face, per OpenAI.
  • OpenAI also said it did not realize its evaluation was connected to the Hugging Face breach until it contacted Hugging Face about credentials exposed during its own investigation.

Threat level: Dalton says the incident shows exactly how attackers will soon weaponize AI agents to target enterprises beyond OpenAI and Hugging Face.

  • "In the near future, we should expect that threat actors will intentionally deploy, optimize, weaponize, and use offensive agent collectives in the manner that we have just described here," Dalton said.

Between the lines: OpenAI has started "consciously slowing down research to enhance security," Dalton said, and has ramped up its monitoring of AI agents during evaluations.

  • OpenAI has also been upgrading its security architecture around the evaluation environment.
  • Dalton recommends agent-created security fixes to keep up with the speed of malicious hackers.
  • He added that defenders should start experimenting with both frontier and open-weight models for these tasks.

What's next: OpenAI says it's planning to release a full post-mortem of the incident in the coming weeks.

The bottom line: Companies need to start embracing autonomous red teaming, automated incident response and automated patching.

Go deeper: AI's alarming new skill: breaking out of the test lab

The bottom line: Companies need to start embracing autonomous red teaming, automated incident response and automated patching.

Go deeper: AI's alarming new skill: breaking out of the test lab

item.title: Tucker Carlson unveils 10-point manifesto amid third-party speculation
item.description:
Tucker Carlson used a highly promoted livestream Wednesday to unveil a 10-point vision for America — defining the worldview of a breakaway MAGA faction increasingly at odds with President Trump.

Why it matters: After vowing last month to "help build a third party," Carlson fueled further speculation this weekend by hosting MAGA dissidents at his home in Maine, where they urged him to run for president in 2028.

  • The former Fox News host stopped short of a formal launch, instead presenting the manifesto as the foundation for "whatever comes next" — a new political order he said could "find all kinds of expressions."

Zoom in: Carlson said any successor to America's faltering political system should begin with a shared understanding of what the country "should be," which he distilled into 10 points.

  1. Fair: The same rules should apply to presidents, federal agents and elites such as Jeffrey Epstein, whose impunity Carlson cast as emblematic of an "Epstein class" enriching itself through a corrupt system.
  2. Sovereign: Carlson claimed Israel pushed the U.S. into the Iran war through "bribery or threat or both," while describing foreign lobbying, corporate control of government and high-interest debt as forms of "slavery."
  3. Productive: America should rebuild farming, manufacturing and craftsmanship while rejecting an economy dominated by finance, real estate speculation, surveillance systems and weapons.
  4. Beautiful: Carlson alleged that urban planners deliberately "uglified" American cities, and portrayed brutalist architecture, graffiti, public drug use and violent crime as deliberate attacks on the public.
  5. Healthy: Carlson embraced RFK Jr.'s food agenda, called for universal sobriety and said widespread use of drugs such as Xanax, Adderall and SSRIs had left Americans "half-addled."
  6. Honest: Government officials should be punished for lying to citizens, and most classified records — including on the JFK assassination and 9/11 — should be opened.
  7. Optimistic: Carlson argued that having children is a biological imperative and the foundation of long-term thinking, while blaming aging and childless elites for policies that disregard future generations.
  8. Wise: Schools should teach how the physical world actually works and what he called unchanging facts about human nature — including innate differences between men and women — rather than credentials, screens and technological fads.
  9. Decent: The U.S. should apologize and pay restitution for killing noncombatants, reverse Trump's "Department of War" rebrand and stop funding allies that commit what Carlson called genocide, citing Israel.
  10. United: Carlson called for halting immigration until the effects of AI become clearer, ending benefits for undocumented immigrants and making English the sole language of federal documents and ballots.

The big picture: Carlson has become the intellectual hub for a small but vocal faction of MAGA exiles who say Trump abandoned the "America First" agenda by launching the Iran war, mishandling the Epstein files and allowing Israel to exert too much influence over U.S. policy.

  • The loose group includes former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, Rep. Thomas Massie and Joe Kent, who resigned as Trump's counterterrorism chief in March to protest the war.
  • The White House dismissed them as an "embarrassing collection of mostly whiny turncoats who dramatically overestimate their influence and relevance," while declaring Trump the "unequivocal leader" of the Republican Party.
